stimuli.title: Bringing Books to the Block
stimuli.text:
(1) For many families, the nearest public library is a long walk or a bus ride away. (2) In some rural counties and crowded cities, that distance keeps children from borrowing books over the summer. (3) Bookmobiles, which are libraries built inside large vans or buses, were created to solve this problem. (4) Today, a single bookmobile can carry thousands of books along with laptops, puzzles and craft kits.

(5) A bookmobile follows a regular schedule, stopping at parks, community centers and apartment buildings. (6) Readers who visit can borrow books, return them at the next stop and sign up for library cards. (7) Some vans also offer free internet access. (8) The earliest vans had no air conditioning. (9) Because the stops are close to home, children who might never visit a library building can still choose new books every week.

(10) Running a bookmobile is not cheap. (11) The vehicle needs fuel, repairs and a driver, and the books must be replaced as they wear out. (12) Supporters say the cost is worth it. (13) Students who keep reading over the summer tend to return to school ready to learn, while students who stop reading often lose some of the skills they gained the year before. (14) A van full of books is a small price to pay.

stimuli.title: Gardens in the Sky
stimuli.text:
(1) On a hot summer afternoon, a black tar roof in New York City can become far hotter than the air around it. (2) That heat rises into the neighborhood and makes nearby buildings work harder to stay cool. (3) A green roof, which is a roof covered with soil and low-growing plants, offers a different approach.

(4) The plants on a green roof shade the surface below them. (5) They also release water into the air, which cools the roof the way sweat cools skin. (6) As a result, the floors beneath a green roof need less air conditioning in summer. (7) The soil also soaks up rainwater. (8) During a heavy storm, this slows the flow of water into city sewers, which can overflow when too much rain arrives at once.

(9) Green roofs have drawbacks. (10) The soil and plants are heavy, so an older building may need a stronger roof before one can be installed. (11) Some plants need regular watering during dry spells. (12) Sedum, a common green roof plant, has small yellow flowers. (13) Many building owners decide that the benefits outweigh these costs. (14) Green roofs are good.

stimuli.title: An Old Neighbor Returns
stimuli.text:
**1** When Henry Hudson sailed into New York Harbor in 1609, the water held something that today's New Yorkers would hardly believe. Oyster reefs covered huge stretches of the harbor floor. For the next two centuries, oysters were so plentiful that street carts sold them the way vendors sell pretzels today.

**2** That plenty did not last. People harvested oysters faster than the reefs could grow back, and by the early 1900s, sewage and factory waste had made the harbor too dirty for the few that remained. Health officials closed the last oyster beds. For most of the twentieth century, the harbor's reefs were gone.

**3** In recent decades, the water has slowly grown cleaner, and a group called the Billion Oyster Project has set out to bring the oysters back. Its goal is to restore one billion live oysters to the harbor by 2035. The work is part science and part teamwork. Restaurants donate the shells left over from oyster dinners. Volunteers clean and cure the shells, and baby oysters, called spat, attach themselves to the old shells and begin to grow.

**4** Why go to so much trouble for a creature most people will never eat? A single adult oyster can filter dozens of gallons of water a day, removing tiny particles as it feeds. A reef also gives fish, crabs and other animals places to hide and find food. Some scientists think that large reefs could even soften the force of storm waves before they reach the shore.

**5** Many of the people doing this work are teenagers. Students at a public high school on Governors Island raise oysters, test the water and dive to check on the reefs. For them, the harbor is not just a view from a ferry. It is a living classroom, and the return of an old neighbor is a sign that a damaged place can heal.

stimuli.title: The Long Way
stimuli.text:
**1** Rosa had ridden the subway to her grandfather's apartment every Saturday for three years, but she had never once made the trip alone. Today her mother had a work shift she could not trade, and after a long talk at the kitchen table, Rosa had won. She was twelve. She knew the stops by heart.

**2** "Text me when you get on, text me when you change trains, and text me when you're at his door," her mother said for the third time, holding Rosa's face in both hands.

**3** "I know, Mami."

**4** On the platform, Rosa felt taller than usual. She stood behind the yellow line exactly the way her mother always did and stepped into the car as if she rode it alone every day. Then, two stops later, the conductor's voice crackled through the speaker. Because of work on the tracks, the train would run express. It would not stop at her station.

**5** Rosa's stomach tightened. She looked around at the strangers in the car, all of them reading, sleeping or staring at their phones as if nothing had happened. For a moment she wanted to call her mother and admit that she could not do this after all.

**6** Instead, she studied the map above the doors. If the train skipped her stop, she could get off at the next one and take a local train back one station. She traced the route twice with her finger to be sure.

**7** Twenty minutes later than planned, she climbed the stairs to her grandfather's building. He opened the door before she knocked, holding his phone. "Your mother called me four times," he said, frowning. Then the frown broke into a grin. "She said you took the long way."

**8** Rosa laughed, and only then did she notice that her hands had stopped shaking somewhere on the stairs.

stimuli.title: The Colors Hiding in a Leaf
stimuli.text:
**1** Every autumn, the hills of upstate New York turn red, orange and gold, and visitors drive for hours to see them. It is natural to think that trees "paint" their leaves new colors in the fall. In fact, some of those colors were in the leaves all summer long.

**2** A green leaf is green because of chlorophyll, a substance that captures energy from sunlight so the tree can make sugar. In summer there is so much chlorophyll that it hides other substances in the leaf, including yellow and orange ones called carotenoids. Carotenoids are the same pigments that make carrots orange.

**3** As autumn days grow shorter, many trees stop making new chlorophyll. The chlorophyll already in the leaves breaks down, and the green fades. The yellows and oranges that were there all along finally show through. Nothing new has been added; something has simply been taken away.

**4** Reds and purples are a different story. Some trees, such as red maples, produce new red pigments, called anthocyanins, in the fall. These pigments form when sugar builds up in the leaf. That is why a stretch of sunny days followed by cool nights, which keeps sugar trapped in the leaves, often brings the brightest reds.

**5** Eventually, a layer of cells at the base of each leaf stem seals the leaf off from the branch, and the leaf drops. The tree rests through the winter, living on the food it stored. In spring it will grow new leaves full of chlorophyll, and the yellows and oranges will hide again until next fall.

stimuli.title: Ice Storm
stimuli.text:
All night the rain forgot how to be rain.

It froze the moment that it touched a thing:

the maple's arms, the mailbox, the long wire

that runs from the pole to our kitchen light.

​

By morning the whole street was made of glass.

The branches bowed as if they were ashamed,

and every twig wore a sleeve of clear crystal

that clicked and chimed whenever the wind moved.

​

My father said the power would be out

until the crews could reach us, maybe days.

We ate cold cereal by the window, wrapped

in every blanket we could find, and watched.

​

Then the sun climbed over the neighbors' roof

and struck the trees, and every inch of ice

caught fire at once, white, gold, a little blue.

Nobody spoke. We had forgotten we were cold.

stimuli.title: In Defense of Doing Nothing
stimuli.text:
**1** Ask a group of seventh graders what they did last weekend, and many will list activities: practice, lessons, tutoring, a birthday party, homework. Ask when they last had an afternoon with nothing planned, and the room may go quiet. Many families work hard to keep children busy. I would like to argue for the opposite: every young person needs regular time to be bored.

**2** Boredom feels unpleasant, and that is exactly why it is useful. When there is nothing to do, the mind starts looking for something. A child stuck indoors on a rainy day may build a fort out of couch cushions, invent a game with a deck of cards or finally open the book that has been sitting on the shelf. No adult planned those activities. The child came up with them.

**3** Busy schedules can crowd out that kind of thinking. A student who moves from school to soccer to piano to homework rarely has to decide what to do next; someone else has already decided. There is nothing wrong with soccer or piano. The problem comes when every hour is filled, leaving no room for a young person to discover what he or she actually enjoys.

**4** Some parents worry that unplanned time will turn into hours of scrolling on a phone. That concern is fair. Screens can fill empty time so quickly that boredom never has a chance to do its work. But the answer is not to schedule every minute. It is to set aside some time that is free of both activities and screens.

**5** None of this requires money or special equipment. It requires only a willingness to let an afternoon stay empty and to resist the urge to fill it. A young person who learns to handle boredom learns something no lesson can teach: how to make an interesting life out of whatever is at hand.

stimuli.title: Letters from the Mill
stimuli.text:
**1** The bell in the tower rang at half past four, and Hannah was already awake. In the three weeks since she had come to the mill town from her family's farm, she had learned that the bell ruled everything: when to wake, when to eat, when to work and when to sleep.

**2** In the weaving room, the looms were so loud that the girls spoke to one another with their hands. Hannah's job was to watch two machines at once and to tie broken threads before a flaw could spread across the cloth. Her fingers were sore, and the cotton dust made her cough. At night she wrote to her younger sister, Abby, but she left those parts out.

**3** Instead she wrote about the things that made her feel grown. She had a wage of her own, and she had already sent half of it home to help pay off the farm. On Sunday afternoons, she walked to the lending library with Mary, the older girl who shared her room in the boardinghouse. Mary had once had a poem printed in a magazine that the mill girls wrote themselves.

**4** "You should write something," Mary told her one evening, nodding at the stack of letters. "You have a way of making ordinary things sound worth hearing."

**5** Hannah laughed and shook her head. Who would want to read about looms and boardinghouse suppers? But that night, after the lamps were out, she lay awake turning sentences over in her mind the way she turned a broken thread between her fingers, looking for the place to begin.

**6** The next morning the bell rang at half past four, as it always did. Hannah rose with the others, but in her apron pocket she carried a folded sheet of paper and the stub of a pencil.

stimuli.title: The Engineer Behind the Engineer
stimuli.text:
(1) When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. (2) Most people know that it was designed by John A. Roebling. (3) Fewer people know how much the bridge owed to his daughter-in-law, Emily Warren Roebling.

(4) John Roebling died in 1869, before construction began, and his son Washington took charge of the project. (5) A few years later, Washington became seriously ill after working in the pressurized chambers beneath the river. (6) Unable to visit the site, he watched the work from a window of his home. (7) Emily carried his instructions to the engineers and brought their questions back to him. (8) To do this well, she studied subjects such as the strength of materials and the stress on cables. (9) Brooklyn is one of the five boroughs of New York City.

(10) Over time, engineers and officials began to bring their questions straight to Emily. (11) Some even came to believe that she was the real designer of the bridge. (12) When the bridge was finished, she was the first person to ride across it in a carriage. (13) Today a plaque on the bridge honors her along with her husband and his father. (14) She did a lot of things.

stimuli.title: A Later Bell
stimuli.text:
(1) In many middle schools, the first bell rings before 8:00 a.m. (2) To arrive on time, some students wake up before 6:30. (3) Doctors who study sleep say this schedule does not match the way a teenager's body works.

(4) During the early teen years, the body's internal clock shifts later. (5) Many teenagers do not feel sleepy until about 11:00 p.m., even if they go to bed earlier. (6) The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. (7) Sleep experts say that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. (8) A student who falls asleep at 11:00 and wakes at 6:30 gets only seven and a half hours. (9) Breakfast is often called the most important meal of the day.

(10) Some families worry that a later start would push sports practices and after-school jobs later into the evening. (11) Bus schedules would also have to change. (12) Schools that have made the switch, however, often report that students are more alert in class. (13) A later bell is a change.

stimuli.title: A Scientist of Many Talents
stimuli.text:
**1** On September 12, 1992, the space shuttle Endeavour lifted off from Florida with seven astronauts aboard. One of them, Dr. Mae Jemison, became the first African American woman to travel into space. For Jemison, the flight was not the start of a dream but the latest step in a life spent following many interests at once.

**2** Jemison grew up in Chicago, where she spent hours at the library reading about science and astronomy. She also loved to dance. At sixteen she entered Stanford University, where she earned a degree in chemical engineering and also studied African American history. Later she earned a medical degree from Cornell University.

**3** Before joining NASA, Jemison worked as a doctor for the Peace Corps in Sierra Leone and Liberia, in West Africa. She cared for volunteers, wrote guides on health and helped with medical research. The work taught her to make careful decisions far from home, a skill that would matter in space.

**4** NASA selected Jemison as an astronaut in 1987. On her mission of about eight days, she served as a science specialist and ran experiments on how the body responds to life without gravity, including studies of bone loss and motion sickness. She also carried small objects that honored people and places she cared about, among them a poster from a dance company.

**5** After leaving NASA, Jemison started a technology company and created an international science camp for students. She has often said that science belongs to everyone and that creativity in the arts and creativity in science come from the same place. Her own life, which has included medicine, engineering, dance and space flight, may be the best support for that idea.

stimuli.title: Fan 3
stimuli.text:
**1** On the morning the oxygen alarm went off, Teo was the only one in the greenhouse. The colony's adults were outside the dome, repairing a solar panel damaged in the night's dust storm. The alarm was not loud. It was a soft, steady chime, the kind meant to warn rather than frighten. Somehow that made it worse.

**2** Teo checked the screen beside the door. Oxygen in the greenhouse was dropping slowly, and the cause was listed in plain letters: FAN 3 OFFLINE. Without the fan, the air from the plants was not reaching the rest of the dome.

**3** He knew where Fan 3 was. He had walked past it a thousand times on his way to water the tomato vines, a gray box humming behind a panel no one ever opened. He also knew the rule his mother repeated every week: never touch a machine you have not been trained on.

**4** Teo pressed the call button. "Fan 3 is down," he said. "Oxygen is dropping."

**5** The speaker crackled, and his mother's voice came through, calm but tired. "We heard. We're twenty minutes out. Is the light on the panel latch red or green?"

**6** He looked. "Green."

**7** "Then the power to it is safe, and it's only a tripped switch. Open the panel. You'll see a black lever marked RESET. Push it up, once. Don't touch anything else."

**8** His hand hovered over the latch. Twenty minutes was a long time for the air to keep dropping. He opened the panel, found the lever and pushed it up. For a second nothing happened. Then the fan shuddered and began to hum, and the chime stopped.

**9** When the adults came in, coated in red dust, his mother looked at the panel and then at him. "You followed the rule," she said, "and then you followed me." She smiled. "That's exactly the right order."

stimuli.title: The Animal That Refuses to Quit
stimuli.text:
**1** Under a microscope, a drop of water squeezed from a clump of moss may reveal a strange little animal lumbering along on eight stubby legs. It is a tardigrade, also known as a water bear. Most tardigrades are less than a millimeter long, but they are famous among scientists for being nearly impossible to kill.

**2** Tardigrades live almost everywhere: in moss on city sidewalks, in mud at the bottom of lakes, on mountaintops and in the deep sea. Like many tiny water animals, they need a thin film of water around them to stay active. What makes them remarkable is what they do when that water disappears.

**3** When its home dries out, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and curls into a tiny, shriveled ball called a tun. Its body loses almost all of its water, and its activity slows so much that it can barely be measured. In this state, a tardigrade can survive for years. When water returns, it can swell up and begin crawling again within hours.

**4** In the tun state, tardigrades have survived conditions that would destroy most living things, including freezing cold, intense heat and high doses of radiation. In 2007, scientists sent dried tardigrades into orbit on a satellite and exposed them to outer space. Some of them survived and later produced healthy young.

**5** Researchers are now studying how tardigrades protect their bodies while dried out. Some have found special proteins that seem to hold the parts of a cell in place, a little like packing material around a fragile package. Learning how these proteins work might someday help scientists store medicines without refrigeration. A creature most people have never seen could end up solving very human problems.

stimuli.title: Why Heron Stands on One Leg
stimuli.text:
**1** Long ago, when the marsh was new, Heron waded on two long legs like any other wading bird, and she was the proudest creature in the reeds. Each morning she stalked through the shallows, splashing so loudly that every fish for a mile knew she was coming.

**2** "Why do you never catch anything?" asked Turtle, who was sunning himself on a log.

**3** "The fish in this marsh are cowards," said Heron. "They hide the moment they see me."

**4** "They do not see you," said Turtle. "They hear you."

**5** Heron puffed out her chest. She did not care to be taught by a creature who carried his house on his back. So she went on splashing, and she went on going hungry, until her feathers grew dull and her wings grew weak.

**6** One evening, too tired to stalk, she simply stood at the edge of the water. She lifted one foot to rest it and stayed perfectly still. The water grew calm. The ripples faded. And a small silver fish, thinking the marsh was empty, swam right between her toes.

**7** Heron caught it in an instant. She stood still again, on one leg, and soon caught another, and another.

**8** The next morning she flew to Turtle's log. "You were right," she said, and it was the hardest thing she had ever said. "Stillness catches more than splashing."

**9** Turtle only blinked his slow eyes. "Wisdom is easy to find," he said, "for anyone quiet enough to hear it."

**10** And that is why, to this day, the heron stands on one leg at the edge of the water, as still as a reed, waiting.

stimuli.title: What the Meadows Do Not Show
stimuli.text:
**1** Each year, millions of people stroll, jog and picnic in Central Park. Its winding paths, meadows and lakes look so natural that many visitors assume the land was always this way. In fact, nearly every hill, pond and stretch of woods in the park was planned.

**2** In the 1850s, New York City was growing fast, and its crowded streets had few green spaces. City leaders decided to build a large public park, and in 1858 they chose a design called the Greensward Plan, by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux. The two men wanted a place where people of every background could escape the noise of the city. Workers moved huge amounts of rock and soil, planted trees by the thousands and dug lakes where there had been swamps.

**3** But the land was not empty before the park was built. Hundreds of people lived there, many of them in a community called Seneca Village. Most of its residents were African American, and many owned their homes, which at the time could give Black men the right to vote in New York. The village had churches and a school.

**4** In 1857, the city took the land for the park and forced the residents to leave. They were paid for their property, but many believed the payments were too low, and the community was scattered. For more than a century, Seneca Village was nearly forgotten.

**5** In recent years, historians and archaeologists have worked to tell its story. Digs in the park have uncovered pieces of dishes, shoes and other objects from village homes, and signs now mark the place where the village stood. The park is still a gift to the city. Its history, however, is more complicated than its peaceful meadows suggest.

stimuli.title: Enough
stimuli.text:
**1** My grandmother never measured anything. When she made dumplings, she poured flour into a bowl until it "looked right," added water until the dough "felt right" and pinched each dumpling closed with a quick twist of her fingers that I could never quite follow.

**2** The summer I turned thirteen, I decided I would learn to make them myself. I brought a notebook into her kitchen and a set of measuring cups from home. "How much flour?" I asked, pen ready.

**3** She looked at the measuring cups the way she might look at a strange insect. "Enough," she said.

**4** For weeks, my dumplings were a disaster. Some fell apart in the boiling water. Others were as thick and chewy as erasers. Each time, my grandmother tasted one, nodded slowly and said, "Again."

**5** I filled pages of my notebook with numbers that never seemed to work twice. The flour on a humid day behaved differently from the flour on a dry one. The dough I made in a hurry came out tougher than the dough I made while listening to her stories about growing up near the sea. Somewhere in those weeks, I stopped writing things down and started paying attention to the dough itself: how it stuck to my palm, how it sprang back when I pressed it.

**6** On the last day of August, I made a batch while she sat at the table. She bit into one, chewed for a long time and set down her chopsticks. "Now," she said, "you don't need the notebook."

**7** I still have that notebook. Its pages are spotted with flour and full of measurements that are almost all wrong. I keep it not for the numbers but as a record of the summer I learned that some things cannot be written down. They can only be learned with your hands, one failure at a time.

stimuli.title: A Dance That Draws a Map
stimuli.text:
(1) A honeybee that finds a patch of flowers cannot draw a map for the other bees in its hive. (2) Instead, it dances. (3) Scientists call this movement the waggle dance, and it tells other bees where to find food.

(4) The dancing bee walks in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side. (5) Then it circles back and repeats the straight run. (6) The angle of the straight run shows the direction of the flowers compared with the direction of the sun. (7) The longer the bee waggles, the farther away the flowers are. (8) Honey is made from the nectar of flowers.

(9) In the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch studied these dances closely. (10) He set out dishes of sugar water at different distances from a hive and watched how the bees that found them danced. (11) His work helped earn him a Nobel Prize in 1973. (12) The dance is amazing.

stimuli.title: Hunting by Ear
stimuli.text:
**1** On a summer evening, a bat swoops over a pond, twists in midair and snatches a moth that a person could barely see. It does all this in near darkness. Many bats find their food not mainly by looking but by listening.

**2** These bats use a skill called echolocation. As a bat flies, it sends out rapid, high-pitched calls, most of them too high for human ears to hear. The sound waves spread out, strike objects ahead and bounce back as echoes. By listening to those echoes, the bat can tell where an object is, how far away it is and even how it is moving.

**3** As a bat closes in on an insect, it speeds up its calls, sometimes to more than a hundred a second. The faster calls give it a sharper picture of its target in the final moments of the chase. Scientists call this burst of sound a feeding buzz.

**4** Not every bat works this way. Many fruit bats, which eat fruit and nectar, rely mainly on their large eyes and keen sense of smell. Their food stays still, so they have less need to track fast-moving targets in the dark.

**5** Some moths have evolved defenses against echolocation. Certain kinds can hear bat calls and dive toward the ground when a bat approaches. Others make clicking sounds of their own that seem to confuse or warn hunting bats. In the dark skies over a pond, a quiet contest between hunter and hunted plays out every night.

stimuli.title: The Empty Case
stimuli.text:
**1** The trophy case outside the gym had held the same silver cup for eleven years: the city chess championship, won by the school's team long before any of the current players had started school. On Monday morning, the cup was gone.

**2** By lunch, the rumors had grown wild. Someone said a rival school had stolen it. Someone else said it had been sold. Deshawn, the chess club's newest member, said nothing. He was looking at the case.

**3** "The glass isn't broken," he said to Ana, the club's captain, when she sat down beside him. "And the lock isn't scratched."

**4** "So someone had a key," Ana said. "That's half the teachers in the building."

**5** "Maybe." Deshawn pointed at the bottom shelf. In the thin layer of dust, there was a clean circle where the cup had stood, and beside it a second, smaller ring, as if something had been set down and picked up again. "Whoever took it put something next to it first. Something round and small."

**6** Ana frowned. Then her eyes widened. "A bottle of polish," she said slowly. "Ms. Okafor polishes the trophies before the spring tournament. She told us last week."

**7** They found Ms. Okafor, the club's adviser, in the art room, rubbing the cup with a soft cloth until it shone. She looked up, surprised at the two breathless students in the doorway.

**8** "I taped a note to the case," she said, and then her face fell. "It must have blown off when they opened the gym doors."

**9** Ana laughed so hard she had to sit down. Deshawn only smiled. He had learned something about chess and mysteries at the same time: the answer is usually in front of you, if you look before you guess.

questions.stem: Which sentence should follow sentence 4 to introduce the main claim of the passage?
options: These rolling libraries are a smart way to keep young people reading all year.
Bookmobiles are larger than most cars, so their drivers need special training.
Every family in the country should live within a short walk of a library.
People have built libraries for thousands of years in many parts of the world.
questions.explanation: The rest of the passage explains how bookmobiles reach readers and argues that their cost is worth it, so the claim is that they keep young people reading. The sentence about every family living near a library makes a different claim the passage never supports.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph?
options: Sentence 6
Sentence 7
Sentence 8
Sentence 9
questions.explanation: The second paragraph is about what a bookmobile offers readers at its stops. Sentence 8, about the earliest vans lacking air conditioning, has nothing to do with that. Sentence 7 fits, since internet access is one of the services.

questions.stem: Which transition should be added to the beginning of sentence 12?
options: For example,
Even so,
As a result,
In the same way,
questions.explanation: Sentences 10 and 11 describe the costs, and sentence 12 says supporters think the cost is worth it. "Even so" signals that contrast. "As a result" would mean the costs caused the support.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 7 uses the most precise language?
options: Some vans also offer free internet and other helpful things.
Some vans also offer many different kinds of useful services.
Some vans also offer internet access that is useful in many ways.
Some vans also offer free Wi-Fi for homework and job searches.
questions.explanation: Naming free Wi-Fi and what people use it for, homework and job searches, gives the reader exact information. Phrases such as "helpful things" and "useful in many ways" are vague.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 14 best concludes the passage?
options: A van full of books is a small price to pay, and its sides can be painted brightly.
Bookmobiles first appeared more than a century ago in several different countries.
A bookmobile costs money to run, but it keeps children reading when school is out.
Some families would rather visit a library building than wait for a van to arrive.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion returns to the claim and the reason behind it: the cost is worth it because children keep reading. The other sentences add a new detail, a piece of history or a point against the claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be added before sentence 4 to introduce the ideas in the second paragraph?
options: Green roofs help keep both buildings and streets cooler and drier.
Many green roofs also include benches and paths for the residents.
Tar roofs cost less to install than almost any other kind of roof.
Some cities ask new buildings to add solar panels to their roofs.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains two benefits: the plants cool the roof, and the soil holds back rainwater. The added sentence names both. The others bring up benches, cost or solar panels, which the paragraph never discusses.

questions.stem: What is the best way to combine sentences 1 and 2 to clarify the relationship between ideas?
options: Because nearby buildings work harder to stay cool, a black tar roof in New York City can become far hotter than the air on a hot afternoon.
On a hot afternoon, a black tar roof in New York City can become far hotter than the air, although that heat makes nearby buildings work harder to stay cool.
A black tar roof in New York City, which makes nearby buildings work harder to stay cool, can become, on a hot afternoon, far hotter than the air.
On a hot afternoon, a black tar roof in New York City can become far hotter than the air, and that heat makes nearby buildings work harder to stay cool.
questions.explanation: The roof heats up first, and that heat then makes nearby buildings work harder, so the sentences join in that order with "and that heat." Starting with "Because nearby buildings work harder" reverses cause and effect, and "although" signals a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem: Which transition should be added to the beginning of sentence 9?
options: In addition,
However,
For this reason,
In other words,
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists benefits, and sentence 9 turns to drawbacks. "However" signals that change. "In addition" would suggest one more benefit.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it distracts from the main idea of the third paragraph?
options: Sentence 10
Sentence 11
Sentence 12
Sentence 13
questions.explanation: The third paragraph is about the costs and problems of green roofs. Sentence 12, about the color of sedum flowers, does not explain any drawback.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 14 best concludes the passage?
options: Green roofs are good, and some people think that they also look much nicer than tar roofs.
Green roofs are heavy, so they will never work on any older building in a city.
Green roofs cool buildings and catch rain, which helps cities in summer and in storms.
Every roof in New York City should be covered with plants by the end of next year.
questions.explanation: The best conclusion sums up the two benefits the passage explains. The others add a new opinion, overstate a drawback the passage says can be fixed, or make a demand the passage never supports.

questions.passage: (1) Every spring, my grandmother plants tomatoes along the back fence. (2) She starts the seeds indoors in March and keeps them on a sunny windowsill. (3) When the nights grew warm enough, she carries the seedlings outside. (4) By August, the vines are heavy with ripe fruit.
questions.stem: Which sentence should be revised to correct an inappropriate shift in verb tense?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: The paragraph is in the present tense, but Sentence 3 begins with the past tense verb "grew." It should read "When the nights grow warm enough, she carries the seedlings outside."

questions.passage: The coach handed the extra practice jerseys to Marisol and I after the game.
questions.stem: Which words should replace "to Marisol and I" to correct the error in the sentence?
options: to Marisol and myself
to Marisol and me
for Marisol and I
to Marisol and we
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of the preposition "to," so it takes the objective case, "me." Test it alone: you would say "handed the jerseys to me," not "to I." "Myself" is used only when the subject is also "I."

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
options: The storm cut the power, we read by candlelight.
The storm cut the power so, we read by candlelight.
The storm cut the power we read by candlelight.
The storm cut the power, so we read by candlelight.
questions.explanation: Two complete sentences can be joined by a comma and a conjunction such as "so." A comma alone makes a comma splice, and no punctuation at all makes a run-on sentence.

questions.passage: The winning goal was scored by Dana in the final minute.
questions.stem: Which revision of the sentence uses the active voice?
options: Dana scored the winning goal in the final minute.
In the final minute, the winning goal was scored by Dana.
The winning goal was being scored by Dana in the final minute.
By Dana, the winning goal was scored in the final minute.
questions.explanation: In the active voice the subject does the action: Dana scored the goal. Each other version still uses "was scored" or "was being scored," so the goal, not Dana, is the subject.

questions.passage: (1) Last year the city opened a new library branch in our neighborhood. (2) Built from recycled steel and glass, visitors often stop to admire the building. (3) Inside, the shelves hold more than twenty thousand books. (4) On weekends, volunteers lead story hours for young children.
questions.stem: Which sentence contains an error in its construction and should be revised?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: In Sentence 2 the phrase "Built from recycled steel and glass" describes the building, but it sits next to "visitors," as if the visitors were built of steel. It could read "Visitors often stop to admire the building, which is built from recycled steel and glass."

questions.passage: (1) The monarch butterfly travels up to 3,000 miles each fall. (2) It flies from Canada to central Mexico. (3) There it spends the winter in fir forests.
questions.stem: What is the best way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between ideas?
options: The monarch butterfly travels up to 3,000 miles each fall, and it flies from Canada to central Mexico, and there it spends the winter in fir forests.
Spending the winter in fir forests, the monarch butterfly travels up to 3,000 miles each fall from Canada to central Mexico.
Each fall, the monarch butterfly travels up to 3,000 miles from Canada to central Mexico, where it spends the winter in fir forests.
From Canada to central Mexico, where it spends the winter, the monarch butterfly travels each fall in fir forests up to 3,000 miles.
questions.explanation: The best version keeps the order of events: the journey, its route, then the place where the butterfly winters, joined by "where." Stringing the ideas together with "and" repeats words, and the version that opens with the winter puts the stay before the trip.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: Mount Marcy, the highest peak in New York, rises 5,344 feet.
Mount Marcy the highest peak in New York, rises 5,344 feet.
Mount Marcy, the highest peak in New York rises 5,344 feet.
Mount Marcy, the highest peak, in New York rises 5,344 feet.
questions.explanation: "The highest peak in New York" renames Mount Marcy and can be removed, so it needs a comma on both sides. Leaving out either comma, or splitting the phrase, breaks the sentence.

questions.passage: (1) Priya and her older sister, Nadia, entered the science fair together. (2) Their project tested which kind of soil helps bean plants grow fastest. (3) The sisters measured each plant every morning for three weeks. (4) Priya told Nadia that she had written down one of the measurements wrong.
questions.stem: Which sentence should be revised to correct a pronoun with an unclear antecedent?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: In Sentence 4, "she" could mean Priya or Nadia, so the reader cannot tell who made the mistake. Naming the person fixes it: "Priya told Nadia that Nadia had written down one of the measurements wrong."

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a hyphen correctly?
options: The museum offers a two hour-tour of its ships.
The museum offers a two-hour tour of its ships.
The museum offers a two-hour-tour of its ships.
The museum offers a tour of its ships for two-hours.
questions.explanation: "Two-hour" is a compound adjective before the noun "tour," so its two words are joined with a hyphen. The noun is not part of the compound, and "for two hours" after the noun needs no hyphen.

questions.passage: (1) The students in Ms. Ortiz's class are building a model of the Brooklyn Bridge. (2) A box of craft sticks and wire sit on each table. (3) Each of the groups has a different section to finish. (4) By Friday, the class hopes to join the sections together.
questions.stem: Which sentence should be revised to correct an error in subject-verb agreement?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: In Sentence 2 the subject is "box," which is singular; "of craft sticks and wire" only describes it. The verb should be "sits." In Sentence 3 the subject "each" is singular, so "has" is correct.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: People are bringing back the oyster reefs that once helped keep the harbor healthy.
The harbor became far too polluted in the early 1900s for anyone to eat its oysters.
Restaurants in the city now give their leftover oyster shells to scientists.
Students who study the harbor learn more than students in regular classrooms.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the loss of the reefs, the effort to restore them and why they matter. Pollution in the early 1900s and the donated shells are details within that story, and the passage never compares students to other classrooms.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 2 contribute to the development of ideas in the passage?
options: It describes how oysters filter water as they feed.
It shows why restaurants began serving oysters.
It explains how the harbor's oyster reefs were lost.
It argues that the harbor is still too polluted now.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes overharvesting and pollution and ends by saying the reefs were gone, which sets up the effort to restore them. Filtering is described in paragraph 4.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the phrase "part science and part teamwork" mainly suggests that the project:
options: is more about having fun than about results
relies on both research and many helpers
began as a high school science fair project
needs more money than it now receives
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow show both halves: the biology of spat attaching to shells and the help of restaurants and volunteers. Nothing in the paragraph is about fun, a science fair or money.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that oyster reefs help other living things?
options: "Restaurants donate the shells left over from oyster dinners." (paragraph 3)
"For most of the twentieth century, the harbor's reefs were gone." (paragraph 2)
"Students at a public high school on Governors Island raise oysters, test the water and dive to check on the reefs." (paragraph 5)
"A reef also gives fish, crabs and other animals places to hide and find food." (paragraph 4)
questions.explanation: Only the sentence about fish, crabs and other animals shows reefs helping other creatures. The sentence about restaurants shows people helping oysters, not the other way around.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, the author most likely views the student workers as:
options: too young to do serious work on the reefs
the main reason that the harbor water became cleaner
an example of how people can help a place recover
visitors who see the harbor only from a ferry
questions.explanation: The author calls the harbor their "living classroom" and ends with the reefs' return as a sign that "a damaged place can heal." The passage credits cleaner water to recent decades, not to the students.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a theme of the passage?
options: Solving an unexpected problem can build a person's confidence.
Children should never ride the subway without an adult nearby.
Family members often argue about small and unimportant decisions.
Plans that are made carefully in advance always work out well.
questions.explanation: Rosa's plan goes wrong, she works out a new route, and by the end her hands have stopped shaking. Her careful plan does not work out, so the passage does not suggest that plans always succeed.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the detail that Rosa "felt taller than usual" mainly suggests that she:
options: is nervous about the strangers near her
is annoyed that her mother worries
is proud to be trusted on her own
is excited to hear from the conductor
questions.explanation: Rosa has just won the right to travel alone and acts "as if she rode it alone every day," so feeling taller shows pride. Her nervousness comes later, after the announcement.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 6 develop Rosa's character?
options: It shows her deciding to call her mother for help.
It shows her solving the problem instead of giving up.
It shows her asking a stranger in the car for directions.
It shows her blaming the conductor for the change.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6 begins "Instead," turning away from her wish to call her mother, and shows her using the map to plan a new route. She does not call or ask anyone for help.

questions.stem: What does the grandfather's reaction in paragraph 7 reveal?
options: He is angry that Rosa arrived so late.
He is worried that Rosa got lost somewhere on the way.
He is surprised that Rosa traveled alone.
He is proud of the way Rosa handled the trip.
questions.explanation: His frown "broke into a grin," and he jokes that she "took the long way," which shows he is pleased with how she managed. The frown is only a brief tease.

questions.stem: What does the final sentence of the passage suggest about Rosa?
options: She was still too frightened to enjoy the visit.
She had been cold during the long ride on the train.
Her fear faded once she had solved the problem.
She was embarrassed that her mother had called.
questions.explanation: Her hands had stopped shaking "somewhere on the stairs," after she had found her way, so her fear eased without her noticing. She laughs, so she is not still frightened.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the idea that trees "paint" their leaves in paragraph 1?
options: to set up a common belief that the passage will correct
to show that trees choose the colors of their own leaves
to describe how visitors feel when they see fall colors
to compare the leaves of trees to famous works of art
questions.explanation: The next sentence begins "In fact" and explains that some colors were there all along, so the author raises the belief in order to correct it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do yellow and orange colors appear in the fall?
options: The tree makes them from sugar trapped in the leaf.
Cool nights turn the green chlorophyll to yellow.
Shorter days let sunlight add new colors to the leaf.
The green chlorophyll fades and stops hiding them.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the chlorophyll breaks down and the yellows and oranges "that were there all along finally show through." Trapped sugar explains the reds in paragraph 4, not the yellows.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how paragraph 4 relates to paragraph 3?
options: It gives another example of the same process.
It explains that red colors form in a different way.
It describes what happens after the leaves fall.
It argues against an idea that is stated in paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens "Reds and purples are a different story": these colors are made new, while the yellows in paragraph 3 were simply uncovered. It does not argue against paragraph 3.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, which kind of autumn weather would most likely bring the brightest red leaves?
options: sunny days followed by cool nights
cloudy days followed by warm nights
rainy days followed by warm nights
cloudy days followed by icy nights
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says sunny days followed by cool nights keep sugar trapped in the leaves, and red pigments form when sugar builds up.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Trees make all of their fall colors from sugar that is trapped in their leaves.
Leaves change color because cold autumn weather freezes the green chlorophyll in them.
Fall colors appear as chlorophyll breaks down and, in some trees, new reds form.
Upstate New York has the brightest fall colors because it has so many maples.
questions.explanation: The passage explains two causes: fading chlorophyll uncovers yellows and oranges, and some trees make new red pigments. Trapped sugar explains only the reds, and the passage never says chlorophyll freezes.

questions.stem: In line 1, the phrase "the rain forgot how to be rain" suggests that the rain:
options: turned to ice instead of staying liquid
stopped falling at some point in the night
fell harder than it ever had before
was warmer than usual for the season
questions.explanation: The next line explains that the rain "froze the moment that it touched a thing," so it stopped acting like ordinary rain.

questions.stem: In the second stanza, the image of branches that "bowed as if they were ashamed" mainly shows that the branches:
options: broke off and fell onto the street
were cut down later by the repair crews
grew in a strange and crooked shape
bent low under the weight of the ice
questions.explanation: Bowing means bending forward, and the twigs are each wearing "a sleeve of clear crystal," so the ice is weighing the branches down. Nothing in the poem says they broke.

questions.stem: How does the mood of the poem change from the third stanza to the fourth?
options: from great excitement to disappointment
from cold, patient waiting to quiet wonder
from fear of the storm to anger about it
from happiness to a feeling of sadness
questions.explanation: In the third stanza the family waits in blankets with no power. In the fourth, the sun lights the ice and "Nobody spoke," a moment of awe.

questions.stem: What does the line "We had forgotten we were cold" suggest?
options: The beauty of the scene held the family's attention.
The power came back on and warmed up the house.
The family had left the window to find more blankets.
The sunlight melted all of the ice on the trees at once.
questions.explanation: The line follows the image of the ice catching fire in the sunlight, so the family was too caught up in the sight to notice the cold. The ice catches the light; the poem never says it melted.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?
options: Storms are dangerous and should always be avoided.
Neighbors should help one another during a crisis.
Even a hard situation can hold moments of beauty.
Families grow closer when they share a simple meal.
questions.explanation: The storm leaves the family cold and without power, yet the poem ends with a scene so beautiful that they forget their discomfort. The neighbors appear only as a roof the sun rises over.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim?
options: Children should quit their sports teams and music lessons.
Young people need regular free time with nothing planned.
Rainy days are the best days for children to read books.
Parents should take away their children's phones for good.
questions.explanation: The author states the claim at the end of paragraph 1: "every young person needs regular time to be bored." Paragraph 3 says there is nothing wrong with soccer or piano, so quitting them is not the claim.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 4 contribute to the author's argument?
options: It gives the main evidence that boredom is useful.
It describes the author's own weekends as a child.
It admits that the author's claim might be a mistake.
It answers a likely objection to the author's claim.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 raises a parent's worry about screens, calls it fair and then answers it with screen-free time. Granting that a worry is fair is not the same as giving up the claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that boredom can lead to creativity?
options: "Many families work hard to keep children busy." (paragraph 1)
"There is nothing wrong with soccer or piano." (paragraph 3)
"No adult planned those activities. The child came up with them." (paragraph 2)
"Screens can fill empty time so quickly that boredom never has a chance." (paragraph 4)
questions.explanation: The sentences from paragraph 2 show a bored child inventing activities with no adult's help, which is creativity. The sentence about screens explains a risk, not a benefit of boredom.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the phrase "crowd out" most nearly means:
options: leave no room for
gather people around
make much louder
speed up the pace of
questions.explanation: The paragraph says that when every hour is filled there is "no room" for a young person to discover interests, so busy schedules push that thinking out.

questions.stem: What does the final sentence of the passage suggest about learning to handle boredom?
options: It is something only wealthy families can afford.
It is a lesson that teachers should add to school.
It is a problem that most people never really solve.
It is a skill that helps a person throughout life.
questions.explanation: The sentence says handling boredom teaches "how to make an interesting life out of whatever is at hand," a lasting skill. The paragraph also says it requires no money, and that "no lesson can teach" it.

questions.stem: Why does Hannah most likely leave her sore fingers and the cotton dust out of her letters to Abby?
options: She is not allowed to write about the mill.
She does not want her family to worry about her.
She has already forgotten how hard the mill work is.
She hopes Abby will come and work in the mill.
questions.explanation: She writes instead about "the things that made her feel grown," such as her wage, so she is choosing to share the good news and spare her family the hard parts. Nothing says she is forbidden to write about the mill.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, the comparison of Hannah's thinking to turning "a broken thread between her fingers" suggests that she is:
options: worried about the mistakes she made at work
too tired to think clearly about anything
planning to quit her job in the weaving room
carefully working out how to begin writing
questions.explanation: At work she turns a broken thread to find where to tie it, and at night she turns sentences over "looking for the place to begin." The comparison shows careful, patient work on her writing.

questions.stem: How does Mary influence Hannah in the passage?
options: She teaches Hannah how to run two of the looms at once.
She convinces Hannah to send her wages home.
She encourages Hannah to see herself as a writer.
She warns Hannah about the dangers of the mill.
questions.explanation: Mary tells Hannah she should write something because she makes "ordinary things sound worth hearing," and that night Hannah begins planning sentences.

questions.stem: How do paragraphs 1 and 6 work together in the passage?
options: Both show the bell, but the second shows how Hannah has changed.
Both describe the weaving room through Abby's point of view.
Both show that Hannah is planning to go back to the family farm soon.
Both explain why the mill bell had to ring so early each day.
questions.explanation: The bell rings at half past four in both, but in paragraph 6 Hannah carries paper and a pencil, a sign that she has begun to see herself as a writer.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Hannah takes pride in earning money?
options: "Hannah's job was to watch two machines at once and to tie broken threads before a flaw could spread across the cloth." (paragraph 2)
"In the weaving room, the looms were so loud that the girls spoke to one another with their hands." (paragraph 2)
"The next morning the bell rang at half past four, as it always did." (paragraph 6)
"She had a wage of her own, and she had already sent half of it home to help pay off the farm." (paragraph 3)
questions.explanation: This sentence appears among "the things that made her feel grown" and shows her helping her family with her own wage. The sentence about her job describes the work, not her feelings about earning.

questions.stem: What is the value of -7 - (-12) + 3?
questions.explanation: Subtracting -12 is the same as adding 12: -7 + 12 + 3 = 8. Treating - (-12) as -12 gives -16.

questions.stem: What value of x makes 3x - 7 = 20 true?
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: 3x = 27. Divide by 3: x = 9. Subtracting 7 instead of adding it gives 3x = 13 and x = 13/3.

questions.stem: A runner covers 3/4 mile every 1/6 hour. At this rate, how many miles does she run per hour?
questions.explanation: Divide distance by time: (3/4) / (1/6) = (3/4) x 6 = 4.5 miles per hour. Multiplying 3/4 by 1/6 gives 0.125, which is the wrong operation.

questions.stem: A circular track has a diameter of 70 meters. Using 22/7 for pi, how many meters is one lap around the track?
questions.explanation: Circumference is pi times the diameter: (22/7) x 70 = 220 meters. The value 110 uses the radius in place of the diameter, and 3,850 is the area.

questions.stem: A coin is tossed and a number cube with faces 1 to 6 is rolled. What is the probability of getting heads and a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: P(heads) = 1/2 and P(5 or 6) = 2/6 = 1/3. For both to happen, multiply: 1/2 x 1/3 = 1/6. The value 1/3 is the chance of the roll alone.

questions.stem: Two buses leave a station together at 8:00 a.m. One bus leaves every 12 minutes and the other every 18 minutes. When do they next leave together?
questions.explanation: The buses meet again after the least common multiple of 12 and 18, which is 36 minutes, so at 8:36 a.m. The value 6 minutes is their greatest common factor.

questions.stem: What value of x makes 4(x + 2.5) = 30 true?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 4: x + 2.5 = 7.5. Subtract 2.5: x = 5. The value 7.5 stops one step short.

questions.stem: The price of a ticket rose from \$40 to \$52. By what percent did the price increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 52 - 40 = 12. Divide by the original price: 12 / 40 = 0.30, or 30%. Dividing by the new price, 52, gives about 23%.

questions.stem: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 8 centimeters and 14 centimeters and a height of 5 centimeters. What is its area in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: Area is half the sum of the parallel sides times the height: (8 + 14) / 2 x 5 = 11 x 5 = 55. Leaving out the half gives 110.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 80 students at a school of 1,200 students, 28 said they ride a bike to school. Based on the sample, about how many students at the school ride a bike to school?
questions.explanation: 28 out of 80 is 35%, and 35% of 1,200 is 420. The sample is random, so its rate is a fair estimate for the whole school.

questions.stem: On a number line, what is the distance between -4.5 and 7.25?
questions.explanation: Distance is the absolute value of the difference: |7.25 - (-4.5)| = 7.25 + 4.5 = 11.75. Subtracting 4.5 from 7.25 gives 2.75, which ignores the negative sign.

questions.stem: Ravi has saved \$45 and earns \$12 for each hour he works. He wants to have at least \$200. Which inequality shows the number of hours, h, he must work?
questions.explanation: He starts with 45 and adds 12 for each hour, so his total is 45 + 12h. At least 200 means greater than or equal to: 45 + 12h ≥ 200.

questions.stem: In a proportional relationship, 6 notebooks cost \$9. What is the constant of proportionality in dollars per notebook?
questions.explanation: Dollars per notebook is cost divided by notebooks: 9 / 6 = \$1.50. The value 0.67 comes from dividing 6 by 9, which gives notebooks per dollar.

questions.stem: Two angles are supplementary. One measures 3x degrees and the other measures (x + 20) degrees. What is the measure, in degrees, of the larger angle?
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180: 3x + x + 20 = 180, so 4x = 160 and x = 40. The angles are 120 and 60 degrees. The value 40 is x, not an angle.

questions.stem: The ages of five campers are 11, 13, 12, 15 and 14. A sixth camper joins, and the mean age of all six becomes 13.5. How old is the sixth camper?
questions.explanation: The first five ages add to 65. Six campers with a mean of 13.5 add to 6 x 13.5 = 81, so the sixth camper is 81 - 65 = 16.

questions.stem: A store sells n shirts for p dollars each and takes \$5 off the whole order. Which expression gives the total cost in dollars?
options: np - 5
5np
n + p - 5
questions.explanation: The shirts cost n times p, and the discount is taken once from the whole order: np - 5. The expression n(p - 5) takes 5 dollars off every shirt.

questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 41 centimeters. Its base is 9 centimeters. How long is each of the two equal sides?
options: 16 cm
25 cm
32 cm
questions.explanation: The two equal sides share 41 - 9 = 32 centimeters, so each is 32 / 2 = 16 centimeters. The value 32 is both sides together.

questions.stem: A jacket costs \$80. It is on sale for 15% off, and then 8% sales tax is added to the sale price. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: The sale price is 80 x 0.85 = \$68. Tax adds 8%: 68 x 1.08 = \$73.44. Taking 15% off and adding 8% in one step (a net 7% off) gives \$74.40, which taxes the wrong amount.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of 18π inches. What is its area in square inches?
questions.explanation: Circumference is 2πr, so 2r = 18 and r = 9. Area is πr² = 81π. Squaring the diameter, 18, gives 324π.

questions.stem: What is the value of $\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) \times \frac{9}{4} \div \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)$?
questions.explanation: First (-2/3) x (9/4) = -18/12 = -3/2. Then -3/2 divided by -3/2 is 1. Two negative factors give a positive answer, so -1 has the wrong sign.

questions.stem: The formula d = rt relates distance, rate and time. A car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What is its rate in miles per hour?
questions.explanation: Solve d = rt for r: r = d / t = 150 / 2.5 = 60. Multiplying 150 by 2.5 gives 375, which is not a rate.

questions.stem: What is the interquartile range of the data set 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 21?
questions.explanation: The lower half 4, 7, 8, 10 has median 7.5, and the upper half 12, 15, 18, 21 has median 16.5. The interquartile range is 16.5 - 7.5 = 9. The value 17 is the range.

questions.stem: Mia and Theo share 84 stickers in the ratio 3:4. How many more stickers does Theo get than Mia?
questions.explanation: There are 3 + 4 = 7 parts, so one part is 84 / 7 = 12. Mia gets 36 and Theo gets 48, a difference of one part, 12.

questions.stem: On a floor plan, 1 inch stands for 4 feet. A rectangular room is 3.5 inches by 5 inches on the plan. What is the actual area of the room in square feet?
questions.explanation: The room is 3.5 x 4 = 14 feet by 5 x 4 = 20 feet, so its area is 14 x 20 = 280 square feet. Multiplying the plan's area, 17.5, by 4 only once gives 70.

questions.stem: In the decimal 0.272727..., the digits 27 repeat forever. Which fraction is equal to this decimal?
questions.explanation: Two repeating digits over 99 give the fraction: 0.2727... = 27/99 = 3/11. The fraction 27/100 is 0.27 exactly, which stops after two places.

questions.stem: Which inequality describes all solutions of -4x + 9 > 21?
questions.explanation: Subtract 9: -4x > 12. Dividing by -4 reverses the inequality: x < -3. Forgetting to reverse it gives x > -3.

questions.stem: A train travels 90 kilometers per hour. How many meters does it travel each minute?
questions.explanation: 90 kilometers is 90,000 meters. One hour is 60 minutes, so 90,000 / 60 = 1,500 meters per minute. Multiplying 90 by 60 gives 5,400, which goes the wrong way.

questions.stem: A box shaped like a right rectangular prism is 12 inches long, 6 inches wide and 4 inches tall. How many cubes with 2-inch edges fit exactly inside it?
questions.explanation: Along each edge the box holds 12 / 2 = 6, 6 / 2 = 3 and 4 / 2 = 2 cubes, so 6 x 3 x 2 = 36 cubes. The value 288 is the box's volume in cubic inches; each cube has a volume of 8.

questions.stem: A box plot of quiz scores shows a minimum of 52, a first quartile of 68, a median of 75, a third quartile of 84 and a maximum of 97. Which statement must be true?
options: The mean score is exactly 75
About half the scores are below 68
About half the scores are 75 or more
The scores have a range of 16
questions.explanation: The median splits the data in half, so about half the scores are at or above 75. A box plot does not show the mean, and 16 is the interquartile range (84 - 68), not the range of 45.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4(3x - 5) - 2(x - 6)?
questions.explanation: Distribute: 12x - 20 - 2x + 12 = 10x - 8. Writing -2 times -6 as -12 instead of +12 gives 10x - 32.

questions.stem: What value of x makes 5x - 3 + 2x = 4x + 18 true?
questions.explanation: Combine like terms: 7x - 3 = 4x + 18. Subtract 4x: 3x - 3 = 18, so 3x = 21 and x = 7. The value 21 is 3x, one step short.

questions.stem: Ana deposits \$600 in an account that earns 4% simple interest per year. What is the balance after 3 years if she makes no withdrawals?
questions.explanation: Simple interest is 600 x 0.04 x 3 = \$72, so the balance is 600 + 72 = \$672. The value \$674.92 compounds the interest each year, which simple interest does not do.

questions.stem: A right rectangular prism measures 6 centimeters by 4 centimeters by 3 centimeters. What is its surface area in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: The faces come in pairs: 2(6 x 4) + 2(6 x 3) + 2(4 x 3) = 48 + 36 + 24 = 108. Counting each face once gives 54, and 72 is the volume.

questions.stem: What is the value of $18 - 3 \times 2^3 + 10 \div 5$?
questions.explanation: Exponent first: 2^3 = 8. Then 3 x 8 = 24 and 10 / 5 = 2. Finally 18 - 24 + 2 = -4. Subtracting 18 - 3 before multiplying gives 15 x 8 + 2 = 122.

questions.stem: Three friends used a \$12 coupon on a restaurant bill and split the rest equally. Each friend paid \$18.50. What was the bill, in dollars, before the coupon? Type the number.
questions.explanation: If b is the bill, (b - 12) / 3 = 18.50. Then b - 12 = 55.50 and b = \$67.50.

questions.stem: Sam's first four test scores are 82, 90, 76 and 88. What score does he need on the fifth test to have a mean of exactly 85 for all five tests? Type the number.
questions.explanation: A mean of 85 on five tests needs a total of 5 x 85 = 425. His four scores add to 336, so he needs 425 - 336 = 89.

questions.stem: Paint is mixed in the ratio 2 parts blue to 5 parts white. How many quarts of blue paint are in 21 quarts of the mixture?
questions.explanation: The mixture has 2 + 5 = 7 parts, so each part is 21 / 7 = 3 quarts. Blue is 2 parts, or 6 quarts. The value 8.4 uses 2/5 of the total, which treats blue to white as blue to total.

questions.stem: Two lines cross. One angle measures (5x - 12) degrees, and the angle vertical to it measures (3x + 18) degrees. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Vertical angles are equal: 5x - 12 = 3x + 18, so 2x = 30 and x = 15. The value 63 is the size of each angle, not x.

questions.stem: What is the value of $(-3)^2 - 2(-4)(5)$? Type the number.

Kim's tablet has 64 gigabytes of storage, and 23 gigabytes are used. Each movie takes 3.5 gigabytes. The inequality 23 + 3.5m ≤ 64 models the space. What is the greatest number of whole movies she can store?
questions.explanation: 3.5m ≤ 41, so m ≤ 11.7. Only whole movies count and 12 would go over, so the greatest number is 11. The value 18 ignores the 23 gigabytes already used.

questions.stem: A data set is 3, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 40. If the value 40 is removed, which measure changes the most?
options: The median
The mean
The mode
The first quartile
questions.explanation: The mean falls from about 10.6 to about 5.7, because 40 pulled it up. The median moves only from 6 to 5.5, and the mode stays at 5.

questions.stem: A store buys a lamp for \$45 and marks the price up 60%. Later it sells the lamp for 25% off the marked price. What is the sale price, in dollars? Type the number.
questions.explanation: The marked price is 45 x 1.60 = \$72. Taking 25% off leaves 72 x 0.75 = \$54.

questions.stem: A prism's base is a right triangle with legs of 6 centimeters and 8 centimeters. The prism is 10 centimeters long. What is its volume in cubic centimeters? Type the number.
questions.explanation: The base area is (6 x 8) / 2 = 24 square centimeters. Volume is base area times length: 24 x 10 = 240 cubic centimeters.

questions.stem: At 6 a.m. the temperature was -6 degrees Fahrenheit. It rose 2.5 degrees each hour. What was the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, at 1 p.m.?
questions.explanation: From 6 a.m. to 1 p.m. is 7 hours, so the rise is 7 x 2.5 = 17.5 degrees. Then -6 + 17.5 = 11.5. The value 17.5 is the rise alone.

questions.stem: Five more than twice a number is the same as 3 less than four times the number. What is the number?
questions.explanation: Write 2n + 5 = 4n - 3. Subtract 2n: 5 = 2n - 3. Add 3: 8 = 2n, so n = 4. The value 8 is 2n, one step short.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red tiles and 6 blue tiles. Two tiles are drawn at random, one after the other, without putting the first back. What is the probability that both tiles are red?
questions.explanation: The first draw is red with probability 4/10. Then 3 red tiles are left among 9, so the second is red with probability 3/9. Multiply: 4/10 x 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. The value 4/25 puts the first tile back.

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 5:3. After 6 more girls join, the ratio of boys to girls is 5:4. How many boys are in the club?
questions.explanation: Let the club have 5x boys and 3x girls. Then 5x / (3x + 6) = 5/4, so 20x = 15x + 30 and x = 6. There are 5 x 6 = 30 boys.

questions.stem: Which three lengths can be the sides of a triangle?
options: 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm
2 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm
5 cm, 7 cm and 11 cm
4 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm
questions.explanation: The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest: 5 + 7 = 12, which is more than 11. In the 4, 5 and 9 set the short sides add to exactly 9, so they lie flat and make no triangle.

questions.stem: If a = -2 and b = 3, what is the value of $\dfrac{a^2 b - b^2}{a - b}$?
questions.explanation: a^2 b = 4 x 3 = 12 and b^2 = 9, so the top is 12 - 9 = 3. The bottom is -2 - 3 = -5, and 3 / (-5) = -0.6.

questions.stem: Lena bought a tablet that was 25% off. She also used a \$15 gift card, and then paid \$120. What was the original price of the tablet?
questions.explanation: If p is the original price, 0.75p - 15 = 120. Then 0.75p = 135 and p = 135 / 0.75 = \$180. The value \$135 is the sale price, before the gift card.

questions.stem: Which sentence should follow sentence 3 to introduce the main claim of the passage?
options: Suspension bridges hang their roads from cables strung between tall towers.
Without her skill and effort, the bridge might never have been finished.
Many other bridges in New York City are now longer than this famous one.
Her husband drew the plans for most of the bridge's towers by himself.
questions.explanation: The passage goes on to show how Emily Roebling kept the project going while her husband was ill, so the main claim is that the bridge depended on her. The sentence about suspension bridges is accurate but is not a claim about her.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph?
options: Sentence 6
Sentence 7
Sentence 8
Sentence 9
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains how Emily became the link between her husband and the engineers. Sentence 9, a general fact about Brooklyn, does not support that idea.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 6 uses the most precise language?
options: Unable to visit the site, he looked at various things from a window of his home.
Unable to visit the site, he stayed at home and was not involved very much.
Unable to visit the site, he watched the work through a telescope at his window.
Unable to visit the site, he followed what was going on in some kind of way.
questions.explanation: "Watched the work through a telescope" tells exactly how he followed the project. "Various things" and "in some kind of way" are vague, and "not involved very much" contradicts the rest of the paragraph.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be added after sentence 10 to support the idea in that sentence?
options: She could answer them with exact figures for the cables and loads.
The towers of the bridge are built of granite and limestone.
Washington Roebling lived for more than forty years after the bridge opened.
Huge crowds walked across the bridge on the day that it opened.
questions.explanation: Sentence 10 says people began bringing their questions straight to Emily. A detail showing that she could answer them with exact figures explains why. The other sentences may be true but do not support that idea.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 14 best concludes the passage?
options: She did a lot of things, and she also liked to ride in carriages around the city.
The bridge cost far more money and took much longer to build than anyone planned.
Everyone in New York already knows about Emily Warren Roebling and her life.
Her work deserves a place in the story of one of the city's great landmarks.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that Emily Roebling's role is less known than it should be, so a conclusion saying her work deserves a place in the bridge's story fits. Saying everyone already knows about her contradicts sentence 3.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph?
options: Sentence 5
Sentence 7
Sentence 9
Sentence 11
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains why early start times leave teenagers short of sleep. Sentence 9 is about breakfast, not sleep. Sentence 11 is in the third paragraph and belongs to the discussion of bus schedules.

questions.stem: Where should sentence 6 be moved to improve the organization of the second paragraph?
options: After sentence 4
After sentence 7
After sentence 8
After sentence 10
questions.explanation: Sentences 4, 5, 7 and 8 build the problem step by step: the body clock shifts, teenagers need 8 to 10 hours, and an early alarm leaves them short. The doctors' recommendation for a later start makes most sense right after that problem is shown, after sentence 8.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be added before sentence 10 to introduce the ideas in the third paragraph?
options: Some schools now serve breakfast in classrooms each morning instead.
Teenagers who sleep well also tend to be in a better mood.
Changing the start time would not be easy for every community.
Younger children often wake up early without an alarm clock.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph raises the problems a later start could cause and then answers them. A sentence saying the change would not be easy introduces those problems. The others bring up new topics.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 12 to support the idea in that sentence?
options: Many students enjoy playing on school sports teams after the school day ends.
In one district, teachers saw fewer students dozing during first period.
Some buses carry both middle and high school students each day.
Most schools in the state close for summer vacation in late June.
questions.explanation: Sentence 12 says schools that switched report more alert students. Teachers seeing fewer students dozing is evidence of that. The other sentences do not show anything about alertness.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 13 best concludes the passage?
options: A later bell is a change, and changes like this can be hard for many busy families to plan around.
Students should simply go to bed earlier so that they can wake up before 6:30.
Some schools may never change their start times, no matter what doctors say.
Even with new schedules to plan, a later bell is worth it, because rested students learn better.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion restates the claim and answers the worry from the third paragraph: the schedules can be planned, and the benefit is better learning. Telling students to go to bed earlier ignores sentence 5, which says many cannot fall asleep sooner.

questions.passage: (1) Last summer, my brother and I volunteered at an animal shelter. (2) Each morning, we fed the dogs and cleaned their kennels. (3) In the afternoons, we walked the older dogs around the park. (4) By the end of August, three of our favorite dogs find new homes.
questions.stem: Which sentence should be revised to correct an inappropriate shift in verb tense?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: The paragraph tells about last summer in the past tense, but Sentence 4 uses the present tense "find." It should read "had found" or "found."

questions.stem: Which sentence uses pronouns correctly?
options: Jamal and her finished the mural before the bell rang.
Her and Jamal finished the mural before the bell rang.
Jamal and she finished the mural before the bell rang.
Jamal and herself finished the mural before the bell rang.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subjective case, "she." Test it alone: "She finished the mural," not "Her finished the mural."

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: After the rain stopped, the children ran outside to play.
After the rain stopped the children, ran outside to play.
After, the rain stopped the children ran outside to play.
After the rain, stopped the children ran outside to play.
questions.explanation: The comma belongs at the end of the introductory clause "After the rain stopped." Without it there, a reader could think the rain stopped the children.

questions.passage: Hanging from the ceiling, the students admired the enormous whale model.
questions.stem: Which revision of the sentence corrects the misplaced modifier?
options: The students, hanging from the ceiling, admired the enormous whale model.
Hanging from the ceiling, the students were admiring the whale model.
Admiring the whale model, the students were hanging from the ceiling.
The students admired the enormous whale model hanging from the ceiling.
questions.explanation: It is the model, not the students, that hangs from the ceiling, so the phrase belongs right after "model." Each other version still says the students were hanging from the ceiling.

questions.passage: (1) The Erie Canal, which opened in 1825, connected the Hudson River to Lake Erie. (2) Boats could now carry goods between New York City and the Great Lakes, shipping costs dropped sharply. (3) Farmers in the west began selling more of their crops in the east. (4) New York City soon became the busiest port in the country.
questions.stem: Which sentence should be revised to correct a comma splice?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 joins two complete sentences with only a comma. Adding a conjunction fixes it: "Boats could now carry goods between New York City and the Great Lakes, so shipping costs dropped sharply."

questions.stem: Which sentence uses parentheses correctly?
options: The Bronx Zoo (one of the largest city zoos in the country opened) in 1899.
The Bronx Zoo (one of the largest city zoos in the country) opened in 1899.
The Bronx Zoo one of the largest (city zoos in the country) opened in 1899.
(The Bronx Zoo) one of the largest city zoos in the country opened in 1899.
questions.explanation: Parentheses close around extra information that the sentence can do without. Removing "one of the largest city zoos in the country" leaves a complete sentence: "The Bronx Zoo opened in 1899."
